Knitting Copilot — NLP Assignment 1 report¶

An NLP system with code-based verification for written knitting patterns. It reads a pattern (semantic parsing into a structured Pattern IR), explains it, adapts it to the knitter's own yarn and gauge, draws charts and keeps count of rows. Language models translate between language and structure; code computes and checks every number.
Repository README.md (setup and run), docs/ (CRISP-DM phase documents), eval/ + results/ (evaluations)
Run the app streamlit run app.py
Re-run this report jupyter nbconvert --to html --execute notebooks/report.ipynb (numbers are read from results/)
LLMs free models only: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (Google AI Studio free tier); earlier runs on OpenRouter free models
Orchestration LangGraph (src/knit_copilot/graph.py)

Contents. 1 Business understanding · 2 Data · 3 System (diagrams, components, walkthrough, live demo) · 4 Evaluation (every component) · 5 Agentic coding setup · 6 Limitations and next steps

1. Business understanding¶

Problem. Knitting patterns are written in a compressed language: abbreviations (ssk, sl1 pwise wyif), nested repeats (*k2, p2; rep from * to last 2 sts), several sizes in one line (CO 88 (96, 104) sts), US and UK terms and imperial units. Knitters struggle to (a) understand a pattern, (b) adapt it when their gauge or yarn differs, (c) see the stitch structure without a chart and (d) keep their place row by row.

Users. Beginners (need plain-English explanations and definitions) and intermediate knitters (adapt patterns to their own yarn, metric units; yarns from the Ukrainian market).

ID Use case Tier
UC1 Explain a written pattern (row by row, with stitch counts and dictionary citations) Must
UC2 Adjust a pattern to the knitter's gauge (repeats kept whole, rewritten in the original style, verified) Must
UC3 Yarn advice: exact yarn or fibre + weight → needles (mm), expected gauge, fibre advice Must
UC4 Charts from a written pattern Must
UC5 Row-by-row tracker in a project: setup → generate working pattern (locked) → knit Must
UC6 Abbreviation knowledge base: lookup and questions Must
— Project setup by chat (LLM tool calls) Must
— Real Ravelry patterns in the evaluation Must
UC7 Validate a pattern (stated vs computed counts) Could (basic version built)
— Multi-piece garments, picking up stitches, mistake helper Should (not built)

Business logic kept in scope (docs/01_business_understanding.md §1.5, implemented in project.py with unit tests):

  • BR1 Stages. Setup fields (yarn, needles, gauge, pattern, size) are editable until Generate working pattern; then the project is locked. Start over creates version N+1 and resets progress after a warning.
  • BR2 Prerequisites. Generating needs pattern, size (if the pattern has sizes), gauge and needles; yarn is optional.
  • BR3 Always available. Explain, lookup, yarn questions and validation never change the project.
  • BR4 Numbers by code. Stitch counts, gauge maths, needle sizes and chart grids are computed in code; LLM output with numbers is shown only after it is checked (re-parse + simulation, or the fact sheet).
  • BR5 Metric only. Imperial input (inches, US needles) is converted by code; output is always mm / cm / per 10 cm.
  • BR6 Grounding. Definitions come from the knowledge base; unknown abbreviations are reported, not guessed.
  • BR7 Yarn table. Brands popular in Ukraine, no Russian producers; each row records its source.
  • BR8 Repeats stay intact. Gauge adjustment rounds to whole repeats instead of breaking a motif.

Out of scope: colourwork, short rows, crochet, languages other than English.

From business needs to NLP tasks

Need NLP task Component
Understand notation semantic parsing (text → Pattern IR) + unit normalisation parser
Explain rows grounded generation with citations explainer
Find definitions retrieval (exact/fuzzy + BM25 + dense, fused) KB retrieval
Recognise a yarn entity linking (typos, aliases, Cyrillic names, ambiguity) yarn linker
Route a chat message intent classification (rules + LLM) router
Fill the project from chat tool calling / slot filling setup agent
Adapt the text constrained rewriting in the original style rewriter
Correct numbers deterministic verification simulator, gauge, charts, tracker

2. Data¶

Sources checked (docs/02_data_understanding.md): Ravelry (API for yarns and pattern search; free pattern PDFs), Craft Yarn Council standards (weights, needle ranges, abbreviations), Ukrainian yarn shops, Kaggle / Hugging Face. No public dataset pairs knitting pattern text with a structured representation, so the labelled data is built here:

  • Knowledge base (data/kb/): abbreviations with aliases (US/UK), stitch arithmetic (consumes / produces), chart symbols, descriptions in our own words and a reference per entry; fibres and techniques.
  • Yarn table (data/yarns.csv): yarns from brands sold in Ukraine (Ravelry API + shop pages, source per row).
  • Synthetic patterns (src/knit_copilot/data/generator.py): 11 templates (scarves, hats, dishcloths, lace, cables, markers…) × 5 writing styles (terse, brackets, verbose, UK, imperial) + typo noise, each with a gold IR and gold stitch counts.
  • Real patterns: 14 free Ravelry patterns chosen by the author (recent and popular, 2022+), 10 in scope and hand-annotated. PDFs, text and gold annotations are copyrighted and stay in git-ignored data/private/; the repo keeps the metadata index and aggregate results.
  • Hand-written eval sets: intents, setup dialogues, KB queries, yarn mentions, yarn questions.

3. System¶

3.1 Data flow¶

Red: NLP components (an LLM is involved, its output is checked). Green: code only. Brown: data.

In [4]:
display(Image(filename=str(ROOT / "docs" / "diagrams" / "system.png"), width=1100))

Why this design. Free LLMs read language well but make arithmetic mistakes and are slow and rate-limited. So the Pattern IR sits in the middle: the LLM's job is to translate text ↔ structure, and a stitch simulator (driven by the knowledge base's stitch arithmetic) verifies every reading by working the pattern stitch by stitch. A reading that does not add up is sent back once for repair, or rejected. Generation (explainer, yarn advisor) starts from a fact sheet built by code and is checked for numbers and citations that are not on it. Gauge adjustment is pure code; the rewriter's text is re-parsed and must simulate to the adjusted counts. A grammar parser reads common notation without any model call (hybrid mode), which keeps the app usable under free-tier limits.

3.3 Components¶

Component Purpose Input → output Model calls Tool calls
Router components/router.py intent of a chat message (11 intents) text, project stage → intent LLM only when no rule applies (prompts/router.md) —
Setup agent components/setup_agent.py fill the project from chat messages + project status → tool calls, reply yes, ≤ 3 rounds per message set_yarn, set_needles, set_gauge, set_pattern, select_size, get_project_status, generate_working_pattern, start_over → project.py
Parser components/parser.py (+ parser_grammar.py) text → Pattern IR pattern text → IR + warnings hybrid: grammar first, LLM fallback with one repair round simulator as verifier
Simulator simulator.py work the pattern stitch by stitch IR, size → rows with ops and counts, errors — —
Explainer components/explainer.py plain-English explanation IR → text with [id] citations yes (prompts/explainer.md), one repair round fact sheet (facts.py), number/citation check
KB retrieval retrieval/search.py abbreviation lookup and questions query → KB entries — (local embeddings bge-small) —
Yarn linker components/yarn_linker.py free-text yarn → yarn table row mention → match / ambiguous / none — —
Yarn advisor components/yarn_advisor.py needles, gauge, fibre advice yarn (or fibre + weight), question → answer yes (prompts/yarn_advisor.md) facts from table + CYC rules
Gauge adjuster gauge.py recalculate for the knitter's gauge IR, size, gauge → adjusted IR, changes — simulator
Rewriter components/rewriter.py adjusted pattern in the original style text + edits → text yes (prompts/rewriter.md) parser + simulator verify; code render as fallback
Charts charts.py knitting chart IR → grid → PNG — —
Project / tracker project.py, tracker.py, db.py stages BR1–BR3, row position project → status, current row — SQLite
Chat graph graph.py wiring: route → one node → END message → reply (+ chart / tracker) via the components trace per node (tracing.py)

3.4 One input through the system¶

Message in the My project chat: "I'm knitting YarnArt Jeans on US 6 needles, my swatch is 22 sts and 30 rows over 10 cm"

  1. Router: the "numbers" rule matches (mm / sts with digits, no pattern notation) → setup, no model call.
  2. Setup agent: the LLM receives the tool list and the current project status and calls set_yarn(name="YarnArt Jeans"), set_needles(size=6, system="us"), set_gauge(stitches=22, rows=30, over=10, unit="cm"), copying numbers and units as written.
  3. Project rules (code): the yarn linker resolves the name to one row of yarns.csv; US 6 → 4.0 mm from a table; the gauge is stored per 10 cm; each tool returns ok + message (in a locked project every setter refuses).
  4. The tool results go back to the LLM, which writes the reply. The project is saved in SQLite. The trace shows route (rule, no LLM) → setup (2 model calls, 3 tool calls); the app shows it under the reply (LLM trace).
  5. Generate working pattern (button or chat): gauge.py finds the closest cast-on that keeps every repeat whole, simulates the adjusted pattern, shows a preview (cast on, width, length) and locks the project; the tracker starts.

from knit_copilot import project, tracker, charts, gauge
from knit_copilot.simulator import simulate
from knit_copilot.display import row_lines

HAT = '''Hat
Sizes: S (M)
Needles: 4 mm
Gauge: 21 sts and 28 rows = 10 cm in stockinette.
CO 88 (96) sts.
Join to work in the round.
Rnd 1: *k2, p2; rep from * to end.
Repeat Rnd 1 3 more times.
Rnd 2: *k6, k2tog; rep from * to end.
BO all sts.'''

p = project.new_project("Report demo")
print(project.set_pattern(p, HAT).message)                       # hybrid: the grammar reads it, no LLM call
sim = simulate(p.pattern, "M")
display(pd.DataFrame([{"Rows": l.rows, "Instruction": l.instruction, "Stitches": l.stitches, "Worked as": l.worked_as}
                      for l in row_lines(p.pattern, sim, grouped=True)]))

4. Evaluation¶

Method. Every component has its own script (eval/eval_<component>.py) and writes results/<component>_<split>.json. Cases have split: dev|test: we iterate on dev and report test. Synthetic and real Ravelry patterns are reported separately. Components are evaluated in isolation where possible (e.g. the explainer gets the gold IR, so parser errors do not count against it), and end to end where it matters (parser on real text). Model availability (free-tier quota, time-outs) is reported apart from accuracy (answered vs accuracy on answered cases).

Choice of metrics. Comparisons are made on behaviour, not surface form: the parser is scored on the simulation of its IR (stitch operations and counts per row), so k to end and k44 count as equal; generation is scored with checkable facts (coverage, grounding, citations); retrieval with recall@3 / MRR; classification with accuracy and macro-F1 plus rule coverage/precision; the setup agent with the final project state (what the user sees) as well as tool sequence and arguments.

4.2 Parser (semantic parsing)¶

Synthetic patterns: the grammar baseline and the hybrid parser read every pattern exactly (dev 36, test 27; marker set 20). This is an upper bound: the grammar and the generator share notation conventions. The LLM parser (Nemotron, dev) was exact on every pattern it answered; its misses were free-tier time-outs and quota (answered 0.944).

Real Ravelry patterns (the parser's test set, 10 patterns). Input is the text extracted from the PDF.

Error analysis and iterations (details: docs/05_evaluation.md §5.11).

  • Grammar 0/10: real patterns write stitches in words ("Knit one, purl until the last stitch", "slip 1 stitch purl-wise with the yarn held in front"), use whole-row phrases ("P all stitches"), prose lengths and PDF line breaks. It was not tuned on these patterns (they are the test set). This is the main argument for an LLM parser.
  • LLM v2 → v3 (exact 0 → 3): three scoring problems treated equal knitting as different (an optional beginning-of-round marker; sl_pw+wyif vs the single stitch sl_wyif; size names "S/M" vs "S/M Adult"), and the parser threw away a correct reading because the pattern gives no row gauge (now a warning).
  • Remaining errors are real: 4 readings do not add up and are caught by the simulator (the user sees "cannot read" instead of wrong numbers); 3 are structurally wrong but add up (an extra pair of rows, a skipped rib section, sections in the wrong order). Next step: check the parse against counts designers state in prose ("you have knitted 23 rows"), which most real patterns contain.

4.3 Knowledge base: lookup and retrieval (UC6)¶

In [12]:
kbrows = []
for sp in ["dev", "test"]:
    o, _ = R(f"kb_lookup_{sp}")
    kbrows.append({"split": sp, "exact lookup": o["exact"]["accuracy"],
                   **{f"recall@3 {m}": o["questions"][m]["recall@3"] for m in ["bm25", "dense", "hybrid"]},
                   "MRR hybrid": o["questions"]["hybrid"]["mrr"]})
display(pd.DataFrame(kbrows).style.format(precision=3))
  split exact lookup recall@3 bm25 recall@3 dense recall@3 hybrid MRR hybrid
0 dev 1.000 0.900 0.622 0.778 0.889
1 test 1.000 0.683 0.783 0.783 0.833

Exact/fuzzy lookup is perfect (typos like k2tgo → k2tog). Question retrieval misses its 0.85 target. Iterations on dev (stopwords, label fixes, richer KB descriptions, stemming) raised BM25 from 0.64 to 0.90 on dev, but BM25 fell on test (0.75 → 0.68): it was fitting the dev wording. Hybrid (BM25 + dense, reciprocal rank fusion) is the most stable across splits and is the default. Why scores are limited: short KB entries; questions describe effects ("no hole", "a ladder") rather than names; 10 test questions (one question = 0.1). Next: a larger embedding model, LLM query rewriting, and a fresh author-written question set.

Linker: the clean test number is 0.938 (one brand-named-twice case, "Garnstudio Drops Air", fixed after seeing it). Unknown yarns are always recognised as unknown, which matters most: a wrong match would give wrong needle advice. Advisor: all facts come from code (yarn label, CYC table, fibre KB), the LLM writes the answer; a first metric error (expecting a needle size for washing questions) was fixed in the metric, not the system. The judge score is not measured.

    o, _ = R(name)
    ex.append({"set": label, **{k: o[k] for k in ["n", "fact_coverage", "citation_recall", "grounded_first", "grounded_final", "structure_ok"]}})
display(pd.DataFrame(ex).style.format(precision=3))
  set n fact_coverage citation_recall grounded_first grounded_final structure_ok
0 synthetic dev (Nemotron) 9 1.000 1.000 0.889 1.000 1.000
1 real, gold IR (Gemini Flash-Lite) 10 0.992 0.975 0.900 0.900 1.000

Iterations: v2 asked for the count after every changing row (a hat crown had been summarised, coverage 0.64 → 1.0); v3 made a citation by name a check failure so the repair round fixes it. On the real patterns one explanation was rejected for the number 7 — which is correct (a 7-stitch repeat worked 12 times + 2 = 86) but not on the fact sheet: the check favours precision and blocks numbers the model derives itself. Fix for a next version: add each repeat block's stitch count to the fact sheet. LLM judge (different model family, on OpenRouter): not run — the free quota was used up; it also needs calibration against human ratings before it can be trusted.

4.6 Gauge adjustment (UC2) and rewriter¶

In [15]:
ga = [{"split": sp, **{k: R(f"gauge_{sp}")[0][k] for k in ["n", "closest_valid", "motifs_kept", "width_within_1cm", "width_error_unavoidable", "length_within_1cm"]}} for sp in ["dev", "test"]]
display(pd.DataFrame(ga).style.format(precision=3))
o, _ = R("rewriter_dev")
display(pd.DataFrame([o]).style.format(precision=3))
  split n closest_valid motifs_kept width_within_1cm width_error_unavoidable length_within_1cm
0 dev 72 1.000 1.000 0.764 1.000 0.847
1 test 54 1.000 1.000 0.796 1.000 0.889
  n verified_llm first_try fallback final_verified style_similarity_llm style_similarity_code_render
0 9 0.778 0.778 0.222 1.000 0.714 0.554

The maths is right every time (the chosen cast-on is the closest count that keeps every repeat whole, checked by brute force). The 1 cm width target is not reachable for large motifs: feather & fan repeats every 18 stitches (≈ 10 cm per step) — every width miss is such a case where no valid count is closer, and the app says so and suggests a different needle size. Rewriter: all LLM rewrites that came back passed the row-by-row check; 2 of 9 were free-model time-outs and fell back to a code-written version, so the final output is always verified. The LLM keeps the original style much better (similarity 0.71 vs 0.55).

These are consistency checks of code against code (chart builder vs simulator), so 1.0 is expected and guards against regressions; on the real gold patterns too (markers, size-dependent repeats). A visual review of five templates found three presentation problems (reading direction labels, motif box alignment, default rows), fixed before these runs.

4.8 Router (intent classification)¶

In [17]:
rt = []
for mode in ["rules", "hybrid", "llm"]:
    for sp in ["dev", "test"]:
        try:
            o, d = R(f"router_{mode}_{sp}")
        except FileNotFoundError:
            continue
        rt.append({"mode": mode, "split": sp, "model": d.get("model"), **{k: o.get(k) for k in ["accuracy", "macro_f1", "rule_coverage", "rule_precision", "llm_calls"]}})
display(pd.DataFrame(rt).style.format(precision=3, na_rep="—"))
  mode split model accuracy macro_f1 rule_coverage rule_precision llm_calls
0 rules dev none 0.436 0.538 0.436 1.000 0
1 rules test none 0.485 0.552 0.515 0.941 0
2 hybrid dev gemini-3.5-flash-lite 0.982 0.982 0.436 1.000 31
3 hybrid test gemini-3.5-flash-lite 0.939 0.938 0.515 0.941 16
4 llm dev gemini-3.5-flash-lite 0.982 0.982 0.000 — 55
5 llm test gemini-3.5-flash-lite 0.939 0.939 0.000 — 33

Rules alone decide 44–52 % of messages with precision 1.0 / 0.94; the LLM handles the rest. Hybrid and LLM-only reach the same accuracy, but hybrid needs about half the model calls — important under free-tier limits. Errors: two borderline labels ("What is blocking?" → yarn advice; "how to read RS and WS" → abbreviation lookup), one real gap ("German short rows" not recognised as out of scope; seen on test only, not fixed), one rule misfire ("Row 12 says 64 sts but I get 62…" → setup). Earlier runs (v2, v3) lost cases to free-tier quotas (OpenRouter 50 requests/day, Gemini 3.5 Flash 20/day); v4 paces requests and uses Flash-Lite, and every case was answered.

The final project state — what the user actually gets — is correct in every dialogue (30/30). The argument and sequence misses change nothing: an extra read-only status call, a yarn name copied with its typo as the prompt asks ("gazal baby wool", which the linker resolves), and "generate my pattern" answered by checking the status first (the test project had no gauge, so generating would have been refused). An eval bug was found on the way (yarns compared by name: "Alize Cotton Gold" vs the table's "Alize Cotton Gold Solids" → now by linked id), and with it a display bug ("DROPS DROPS Karisma").

5. Agentic coding setup¶

The system was built with an AI coding agent (Claude Code) steered by instruction files, not only by chat prompts:

File What it controls
AGENTS.md framing (NLP system with code verification), tiers and their order, CRISP-DM rules ("no component without its eval", iterate on dev / report test, never copy eval cases into prompts, never edit labels to raise a score), division of labour (LLM vs code), architecture and module layout, data and copyright rules, tech stack, definition of done, don'ts
CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md; Claude-specific rules: use the project skills, read the last log entries at the start of a session, read only relevant files, read the IR schema before parser/simulator/chart work
docs/CONVENTIONS.md shared contracts: Pattern IR schema, intents, setup tools
.claude/skills/ repeatable procedures (below) instead of re-explaining them in chat
docs/crisp-dm-log.md one entry per task: phase, what, why, numbers, next step; read at the start of each session (context recovery)
In [20]:
import re
sk = []
for f in sorted((ROOT / ".claude" / "skills").glob("*/SKILL.md")):
    t = f.read_text()
    desc = re.search(r"^description:\s*(.+)$", t, re.M)
    sk.append({"skill": f.parent.name, "description": (desc.group(1).strip() if desc else "")[:150]})
display(pd.DataFrame(sk))
log = (ROOT / "docs" / "crisp-dm-log.md").read_text()
entries = [e for e in re.findall(r"^## (\S+) — (.+?) — (.+)$", log, re.M) if e[0][:1].isdigit()]
loops = sum(1 for _, ph, _ in entries if ("4" in ph and "5" in ph))
revisions = sum(1 for _, ph, _ in entries if "revision" in ph)
print(f"CRISP-DM log (docs/crisp-dm-log.md): {len(entries)} entries, each with phase, what, why, numbers and next step.")
print(f"Path: Business → Data → Data preparation (parts A–D) → Modeling ⇄ Evaluation ({loops} combined iterations) "
      f"→ Data understanding revised {revisions}× for the real patterns → Deployment (app, report).")
skill description
0 add-abbreviation Add or fix entries in the knitting abbreviation knowledge base (data/kb/abbr...
1 add-component Scaffold a new Knitting Copilot component (module + Pydantic I/O + prompt fi...
2 annotate-ravelry-pattern Turn a free Ravelry pattern the user downloaded into gold evaluation labels ...
3 crisp-dm-checkpoint Append a dated entry to docs/crisp-dm-log.md summarising what was done, why,...
4 generate-eval-cases Create labelled evaluation cases (JSONL) for a Knitting Copilot component: s...
5 run-eval Run one or all Knitting Copilot component evaluations, compare with the prev... 
CRISP-DM log (docs/crisp-dm-log.md): 26 entries, each with phase, what, why, numbers and next step.
Path: Business → Data → Data preparation (parts A–D) → Modeling ⇄ Evaluation (7 combined iterations) → Data understanding revised 3× for the real patterns → Deployment (app, report).

What the instruction files changed in practice (examples from the log):

  • Test discipline. When the grammar parser scored 0/10 on real patterns, the rule "real patterns are the test set" kept the agent from tuning it on them; the finding was reported instead. Likewise the router's short-rows gap.
  • Labels are not edited to raise scores. Where gold labels and system behaviour disagreed (setup agent "gazal baby wool"), the label was kept and the disagreement documented; real label errors were fixed only with a written reason (KB lean questions).
  • Numbers by code. Every LLM component got a code-side check (simulation, fact sheet, re-parse) because AGENTS.md forbids showing unchecked numbers.
  • Copyright. Ravelry text and gold annotations stay in data/private/; eval scripts avoid writing pattern text (e.g. explanations of real patterns are not saved).
  • Where the agent needed correcting: the author steered scope (metric only, Ukrainian yarns, Ravelry patterns as a Must), reviewed data choices (modern patterns), and flagged UI problems (row table, setup flow) that metrics did not show.

6. Limitations and next steps¶

  • Real-pattern parsing is the weakest point (3/10 exact; 4 more rejected safely). Next: verify against counts stated in prose, add markers/pick-ups to the grammar, few-shot with synthetic examples of prose styles.
  • Free-tier models shape the design (hybrid router and parser, caching, pacing) and limit evaluation volume; the LLM judge for explanation/advice quality was not run and needs human calibration.
  • Retrieval misses the 0.85 target on questions; small test sets (10–33 cases) make single errors move scores a lot.
  • Should tier (multi-piece garments, picking up stitches, mistake helper) was not built.
